title: DFW Airport Scraps Islamic Footwashing Station Plan After Texas Governor Threatens Funding Review
excerpt: Governor Abbott calls ablution facilities at Texas airports illegal religious discrimination, launches state grant review and refers DFW and Houston airports to the U.S. DOT.
body:
• Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport abandoned its plan to install Islamic ablution (wudu) washing stations in Terminal D after Texas Governor Greg Abbott threatened to revoke state grants.
  • Abbott referred both DFW and Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport to the U.S. Department of Transportation for investigation, calling the facilities "illegal religious discrimination."
  • The $300,000 privately registered project had been under internal review and was scrapped amid elevated public scrutiny.
  • Similar ablution facilities and interfaith spaces already exist at major U.S. airports including Chicago O'Hare and Indianapolis.

Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport has scrapped a proposal to install Islamic ablution washing stations in its international terminal after Texas Governor Greg Abbott launched a review of state funding to the airport, calling the plan "illegal religious discrimination."

DFW told Fox News Digital on Friday that while it had been evaluating an internal proposal to add wudu ablution stations on the pre-security side of Terminal D, it accelerated the review due to public attention and decided not to proceed.

"DFW was in the process of evaluating an internal proposal to add a set of ablution washing stations on the pre-security side of Terminal D, the international terminal. The airport accelerated its review due to elevated public interest this week and has determined not to proceed with the project as it would not deliver the originally anticipated operational benefits."

— DFW Airport spokesperson

Abbott's Intervention

Governor Abbott announced Friday that he has directed a review of all state grants issued to entities operating DFW and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston for possible revocation and denial of future funding. He also referred both airports to the U.S. Department of Transportation for investigation.

https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2088415472823718207

"Government-owned airports cannot favor one religion over all others. DFW plans to install Islamic wudu washing facilities are illegal," Abbott wrote on X. "Texas will not allow illegal religious discrimination at taxpayer-funded facilities."

In letters to DFW CEO Christopher McLaughlin and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Abbott argued that the ablution facilities "appear designed to single out one subset of the population for special treatment based on religion." He cited both federal and state constitutional provisions prohibiting government facilitation of religious discrimination.

Project Details

The project was officially registered with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation on July 31. The filing listed the project as privately funded with an estimated cost of $300,000, though DFW later said both details contained errors by the airport's outside design firm.

The airport clarified that the actual cost would have been closer to $120,000 and that airport funds — not private donations — would have covered the work. DFW emphasized that it does not use taxpayer dollars for operations, instead relying on revenue from parking and concessions.

Katie Chaumont, DFW's assistant vice president of communications, had said earlier in the week that the airport already offered an ablution station on the post-security side of Terminal D "for years without concerns" and was simply evaluating an expansion to pre-security restrooms.

The Broader Debate

Abbott's office noted that Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport already has an ablution facility with an adjoining prayer room "furnished with copies of the Quran, prayer rugs, prayer beads and a turbah," a small clay tablet used in some Islamic prayer traditions.

Similar low-level ablution basins and interfaith prayer spaces exist at other major U.S. airports, including Chicago O'Hare and Indianapolis, without controversy. Conservative activist Ryan Fournier defended the stations on social media, arguing the plan was about "basic airport management" rather than religious ideology.

"People washing their feet in standard bathroom sinks creates soaked, slippery floors and breaks the counters. Low-level wudu basins keep the restrooms dry and safe for everyone," Fournier wrote.

Diaspora Impact

The episode has drawn attention from South Asian and Muslim American communities who frequent DFW, one of the busiest international hubs in the United States. Wudu — the Islamic ritual washing of hands, face, and feet before prayer — is practiced by millions of Muslim travelers daily, and the debate over public accommodation for the practice touches broader questions about religious freedom in government-owned spaces.

What's Next

Abbott's office said recipients of state grants must certify compliance with laws prohibiting discrimination. The governor has urged Secretary Duffy to launch a federal review and "take appropriate corrective action." Whether the U.S. DOT will act on the referral remains to be seen.
nri_angle: The debate over ablution facilities at DFW Airport raises questions about religious accommodation for South Asian and Muslim American travelers at U.S. airports.
